# Pie charts {#sec-pie-charts}

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
library(scales)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)
# fonts ----
library(extrafont)
library(sysfonts)
source("_common.R")
# use font
showtext::showtext_auto()
# set theme
ggplot2::theme_set(fmggp2::theme_koosh(
    base_size = 14))
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="simple"}
## Theme: `theme_koosh()`

Graphs in this chapter use `fmggp2::theme_koosh()`, built from a tri color Koosh ball: a white background, an orange frame, orange, purple, and black filament marks, peach and lilac accents, and an Arial Rounded title.
:::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="false" icon=false}

<br>

```{r}
#| label: full_code_display
#| fig-asp: 1
#| dev.args: !expr list(bg = "#FFFFFF")
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| out-height: '60%'
#| out-width: '60%'
#| fig-align: right
library(ggplot2)
library(ggpubr)
library(dplyr)
set.seed(1993)
koosh_balls <- tibble(
  ball_id = 1:200,
  style = sample(c("Tri color", "Rainbow", "Neon", "Glow"),
    size = 200, replace = TRUE, prob = c(1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/8)))
koosh_pie <- koosh_balls |>
  count(style, name = "cnt") |>
  mutate(
    perc = cnt / sum(cnt),
    style = factor(style,
      levels = c("Tri color", "Rainbow", "Neon", "Glow"))) |>
  arrange(style)
pie_labels <- paste0(round(100 * koosh_pie$perc), "%")
pie_theme <- fmggp2::theme_koosh(base_size = 14) +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank(), axis.title = element_blank(),
        axis.ticks = element_blank(), panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "bottom")
labs_pie <- labs(
  title = "Koosh balls",
  caption = "Simulated data",
  subtitle = "Styles sold at one toy store",
  fill = NULL)
ggp2_pie <- ggpubr::ggpie(koosh_pie,
          x = "perc", label = pie_labels,
          lab.pos = "in", lab.font = "#FFFFFF",
          fill = "style", color = "white") +
    pie_theme

ggp2_pie +
  labs_pie
```

::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #02577A;"}
**Requirements:**
:::

::: {style="font-size: 1.05em; color: #282b2d;"}
**✅ a categorical variable**
:::

::::

## Description

*“In general, pie charts work well when the goal is to emphasize simple fractions, such as one-half, one-third, or one-quarter.”*

*“They also work well when we have very small datasets.”* - [Claus O. Wilke, Fundamentals of Data Visualization (2019)](https://clauswilke.com/dataviz/)

A pie chart shows how big each part of a whole is, by cutting a round space into pieces like a pie.[^slices] Each piece stands for one group in a column,[^categorical] and the size of the piece shows how much of the whole that group has.[^proportions] We can make pie charts with the code in [`ggpubr`.](https://rpkgs.datanovia.com/ggpubr/)[^ggpubr]

## Set up

::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**PACKAGES:**
:::

Bring in the code we'll use.[^packages]


::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: pkg_code_pie
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| results: hide
install.packages("ggpubr")
library(ggpubr)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr) # for tibble() and data manipulation
```
:::

::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**DATA:**
:::

A [Koosh ball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koosh_ball) is a ball made of many long hairs that is easy to catch but does not come back up when it hits the ground. In the ten years before 2000, Koosh balls came in more styles than anyone needed. Tri color balls have three colors, rainbow balls have many colors, neon balls have very strong colors, and glow balls give off light in the dark. We'll make up[^simulate] the styles of 200 Koosh balls sold at one store with `sample()`. The chances[^probabilities] are simple, and we picked them that way: one in two, one in four, one in eight, and one in eight. Then we find how many balls have each style (`cnt`)[^count] and what part of all 200 balls that is (`perc`).[^perc] Starting with `set.seed()`[^seed] means you'll get the same 200 Koosh balls every time you run the code below.

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: data_code_pie
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
set.seed(1993) # same 200 Koosh balls every time the code runs
koosh_balls <- tibble(
  ball_id = 1:200, # 200 different Koosh balls, one row each
  style = sample(
    c("Tri color", "Rainbow", "Neon", "Glow"), # four styles
    size = 200, replace = TRUE, # one style for each ball
    prob = c(1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/8) # half are Tri color
    )
  )
koosh_pie <- koosh_balls |>
  count(style, name = "cnt") |> # balls of each style
  mutate(
    perc = cnt / sum(cnt), # share of all 200 balls
    style = factor(style,
      levels = c("Tri color", "Rainbow", "Neon", "Glow")) # most to least common
    ) |>
  arrange(style)
glimpse(koosh_pie)
```
:::

## Distribution

A pie chart cuts a whole into pieces, so it only makes sense when the pieces add up to one thing (here, 200 Koosh balls). Pie charts are easiest to read when each piece is a simple part of the whole,[^fractions] and because we picked those parts in `sample()`, we know what each piece should look like. Below we'll move from the Koosh balls, to a graph, to the rule behind it.[^formula]

::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**COUNT IT:**
:::

Start with the first ten Koosh balls.

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: count_values_pie
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
head(koosh_balls$style, 10)
```
:::

Finding how many of all 200 balls have each style, and putting each number next to the number we'd expect[^expected] (200 times its chance), shows how close our made up balls come.

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: count_summary_pie
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
koosh_pie |>
  mutate(expected = 200 * c(1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/8))
```
:::

::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**DRAW IT:**
:::

A bar model sets the 200 Koosh balls out in a line. Tri color balls take up about half the bar, rainbow balls take up about half of what is left, and neon and glow balls share the rest.

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: draw_bar_model_pie
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
#| fig-asp: 0.45
ggplot(data = koosh_pie, aes(x = cnt, y = "200 Koosh balls",
    fill = style)) +
  geom_col(position = position_stack(reverse = TRUE)) +
  geom_text(aes(label = cnt), color = "#FFFFFF",
    position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5, reverse = TRUE)) +
  labs(x = "Koosh balls", y = NULL, fill = "Style")
```
:::

A pie chart takes the same bar and joins its two ends to make a round pie.[^circle] Below, the pie on the left uses the chances from `sample()` just as we gave them, and the pie on the right uses the numbers we made up. The tri color piece covers about half of each pie, and the rainbow piece covers about half of what is left.

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: draw_pie
#| fig-asp: 1
#| dev.args: !expr list(bg = "#FFFFFF")
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
#| layout-ncol: 2
expected_pie <- koosh_pie |>
  mutate(perc = c(1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/8))
ggpubr::ggpie(expected_pie, x = "perc",
    label = paste0(round(100 * expected_pie$perc, 1), "%"),
    lab.pos = "in", lab.font = "#FFFFFF",
    fill = "style", color = "white") +
  labs(title = "Expected", fill = NULL) +
  pie_theme

ggpubr::ggpie(koosh_pie, x = "perc",
    label = paste0(round(100 * koosh_pie$perc, 1), "%"),
    lab.pos = "in", lab.font = "#FFFFFF",
    fill = "style", color = "white") +
  labs(title = "Simulated", fill = NULL) +
  pie_theme
```
:::

::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**NAME IT:**
:::

Each Koosh ball gets one of four styles by chance,[^draw] so the four numbers follow a [rule for picking one of many kinds, again and again](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multinomial_distribution):[^multinomial]

$$
(N_{\text{tri color}}, N_{\text{rainbow}}, N_{\text{neon}}, N_{\text{glow}}) \sim \text{Multinomial}\left(200, \; \left(\tfrac{1}{2}, \tfrac{1}{4}, \tfrac{1}{8}, \tfrac{1}{8}\right)\right)
$$

How wide a piece opens at the middle of the pie[^angle] is its share of the 360 degrees around the pie: $\tfrac{1}{2}$ is 180 degrees, $\tfrac{1}{4}$ is 90 degrees, and each $\tfrac{1}{8}$ is 45 degrees. Simple parts like these line up with places our eyes already know from the face of a watch (half past the hour, 15 minutes past),[^clock] which is why pie charts work best with them.

Each share we made up moves around its chance by about $\sqrt{p(1 - p) / 200}$:[^se] about 3.5 percent of the balls for the tri color piece and 2.3 percent for the neon and glow pieces.[^points] That's why our pieces are close to the ones we expect but not the same. Try changing 200 to 20 in both `ball_id = 1:200` and `size = 200`, and the pieces move much farther from the simple parts.


## Grammar

::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**CODE:**
:::

  -   Make the words that go on the pieces (`pie_labels`) with `paste0()`[^pie-labels]

  -   `ggpie()` gives the graph its own look,[^theme] so make `pie_theme` to bring back the look of this book (and take away the words and small marks on each axis and the lines behind the pie)[^axis-parts]

  -   Make the words around the graph[^labels] with `labs()`

  -   Give the data to `ggpubr::ggpie()`

  -   Give `"perc"` to `x`

  -   Give `pie_labels` to `label`

  -   Give `"in"` to `lab.pos`

  -   Give white (`"#FFFFFF"`) to `lab.font` and `"white"` to `color`

  -   Give `"style"` to `fill`

  -   Add `pie_theme` (which also moves the key[^legend] below the pie)

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: code_graph_pie
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| out-height: '100%'
#| out-width: '100%'
pie_labels <- paste0(round(100 * koosh_pie$perc), "%")
pie_theme <- fmggp2::theme_koosh(base_size = 14) +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank(), axis.title = element_blank(),
        axis.ticks = element_blank(), panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "bottom")
labs_pie <- labs(
  title = "Koosh balls",
  caption = "Simulated data",
  subtitle = "Styles sold at one toy store",
  fill = NULL)

ggp2_pie <- ggpubr::ggpie(koosh_pie,
          x = "perc", label = pie_labels,
          lab.pos = "in", lab.font = "#FFFFFF",
          fill = "style", color = "white") +
    pie_theme

ggp2_pie +
  labs_pie
```
:::



::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**GRAPH:**
:::

```{r}
#| label: create_graph_pie
#| fig-asp: 1
#| dev.args: !expr list(bg = "#FFFFFF")
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| out-height: '100%'
#| out-width: '100%'
#| layout-nrow: 1
pie_labels <- paste0(round(100 * koosh_pie$perc), "%")
pie_theme <- fmggp2::theme_koosh(base_size = 14) +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank(), axis.title = element_blank(),
        axis.ticks = element_blank(), panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "bottom")
labs_pie <- labs(
  title = "Koosh balls",
  caption = "Simulated data",
  subtitle = "Styles sold at one toy store",
  fill = NULL)

ggp2_pie <- ggpubr::ggpie(koosh_pie,
          x = "perc", label = pie_labels,
          lab.pos = "in", lab.font = "#FFFFFF",
          fill = "style", color = "white") +
    pie_theme

ggp2_pie +
  labs_pie
```

[^slices]: Slices. Each slice is one level of the variable.

[^categorical]: A categorical variable.

[^proportions]: The proportion of the total for each category.

[^ggpubr]: The `ggpubr` package, which builds on `ggplot2`.

[^packages]: Install and load the packages.

[^simulate]: Simulate.

[^probabilities]: The probabilities in the `prob` argument (simple fractions: 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, and 1/8).

[^count]: The count for each style.

[^perc]: The proportion of all 200 balls.

[^seed]: Setting the random seed.

[^fractions]: A simple fraction, such as one half, one quarter, or one eighth.

[^formula]: The formula.

[^expected]: The expected count.

[^circle]: A circle.

[^draw]: Each ball is one independent draw from the four styles.

[^multinomial]: A multinomial distribution of the four counts.

[^angle]: The angle of the slice.

[^clock]: Clock positions: half past and quarter past.

[^se]: The standard error of a proportion, where $p$ is the probability for that style.

[^points]: Percentage points.

[^pie-labels]: The slice labels.

[^theme]: Its own theme.

[^axis-parts]: The axis text, axis ticks, and grid lines.

[^labels]: The labels (title, subtitle, and caption).

[^legend]: The legend.
